implementation_notes: insta supplies the loop: assertion macros compare against a committed .snap file, a mismatch writes <name>.snap.new beside it, and the approval step is cargo insta review (or cargo insta accept) which shows the diff and promotes the new value; INSTA_UPDATE controls whether new snapshots are written at all, and the crate detects CI and refuses to write there. Use assert_yaml_snapshot!/assert_json_snapshot! on a serde value to pin the observable projection of a legacy struct rather than its Debug output, and redactions for volatile fields. The hand-written variant stays relevant only when the artefact comes from a build script or binary rather than an in-test value.
pitfalls: Test binaries run in parallel and insta writes .snap.new next to the snapshots; concurrent writers on one snapshot collide, so review runs should be single-threaded or use distinct names.
f64 formatting, HashMap iteration order and generated ids are not stable; redact or normalize them or the snapshot fails intermittently.
.snap.new files are easy to commit by accident; keep them out of version control and let CI fail when they appear.

variants.name: insta inline snapshots in the test source
variants.implementation_notes: The inline form keeps the reference in the source: assert_snapshot!(value, @"") is updated in place by cargo insta review, which rewrites the macro invocation with the recorded value. It suits compact, stable outputs because the expectation is visible next to the assertion and travels with the code in review; for large or frequently regenerated artefacts the file-backed variant is easier to diff and to regenerate.
pitfalls: Source-rewriting snapshots require rustfmt-compatible formatting and a writable checkout; a CI job must never run the review step.
Very large inline values bloat source files and slow compilation of the test crate; move them to .snap files.
